screens.title: Calling Read-Only Smart Contract Functions
screens.subtitle: Use Web3.js to query view and pure functions without sending transactions

narration.text: In this lesson we'll focus on calling read-only smart contract functions from a dApp. Read-only functions—those marked view or pure in Solidity—let your application ask the contract for information without creating a blockchain transaction. That means you do not pay gas, you do not change the chain, and results are returned immediately from the node you're connected to. You will learn the difference between the call method and send, how to handle results that come back as string representations of large integers, and common pitfalls like forgetting to await a Promise or accidentally using send for a view function. We'll walk through concrete code: calling a Storage. retrieve function and reading a Counter. getCount value, and we will include the small hands-on activity that reads the first Ganache account balance. By the end you'll know when to use call, how to read and convert returned values safely, and how these read-only queries power dynamic frontends. Think about one place in your app where you currently poll state: could that be a call instead of a transaction?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use contract.methods.myFunction().call() to query contract data instantly and without gas; treat returned integers as strings/BigNumbers and handle them safely.

screens.title: What makes a function read-only?
screens.subtitle: Understanding view and pure in Solidity and why calls are non-destructive

narration.text: A read-only function is one that does not change the blockchain state. In Solidity this is expressed as view or pure. A view function may read state variables from the contract but guarantees it won't modify them. A pure function goes further: it cannot read or modify any contract state and performs only calculations on its inputs. This distinction matters because when you call a view or pure function from your frontend using Web3. js, the call runs on a node locally and does not create a transaction. No transaction means no gas is spent and no block confirmation is required, which keeps your UI fast and predictable. For example, a function that returns a stored balance is view because it reads a state variable; a function that computes the square of a number from an input without reading storage is pure. A common misconception is thinking view means the node will lock that state for consistency; it does not — it's a local read on the node's view of the chain. To check whether a function is safe to call without gas, confirm its Solidity signature includes view or pure. Reflect: when you need a fresh UI value, would a read-only call suffice, or does the action need to change state and therefore require a transaction?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: view reads state without writing; pure neither reads nor writes state. Both are safe to call with call().

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What makes a function read-only?
Definition

view vs pure

A concise claim: view reads contract state, pure does not even read state; both are safe to call without gas.

Examples
  • view: function retrieve() public view returns (uint256)
  • pure: function add(uint a, uint b) public pure returns (uint)
Common misconception

Calling a view function does not lock or alter blockchain state; it is a private local read on the node and returns the node's current state snapshot.

Analogy

Think of call() as asking a librarian for a copy of a page: you get the information without changing the book. send() is like submitting a new edition for the library — that changes the collection and costs resources.

When to use

Any time you only need to read data for display or decision-making in the frontend.

When not to

If your action must change storage, emit events, or transfer tokens, you must send a transaction.

Key Takeaway

Confirm function visibility and mutability in Solidity: view or pure means it's safe to call() without gas.

screens.title: call() versus send()
screens.subtitle: Behavior, cost, and when to choose each method

narration.text: call and send are the two common ways to invoke contract functions via Web3. js, and they serve very different purposes. call executes the function locally on the connected node and returns the result immediately without creating a transaction. There is no gas cost and no state change. send constructs and broadcasts a transaction to change the blockchain state; it consumes gas and requires miners to include the transaction in a block before you have a final result. Use call for queries like reading a balance or checking an owner, and use send for operations like transferring a token, incrementing a counter, or modifying storage. A frequent error is accidentally using send for a function declared view; this will create a transaction that likely fails and wastes gas. Another pitfall is not awaiting the Promise returned by call, which leaves you with an unresolved Promise object instead of the actual value. Practically, your UI should call state-reading functions frequently for display, while state-changing actions should be guarded with confirmations and gas estimates. Ask yourself: does this action need to change the contract, or does it only need to read current values?

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: call() = local read, no gas, immediate. send() = state change, gas required, transaction lifecycle.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › call() vs send()
call()

Local read, no gas

Executes on the node, returns a Promise with the result. Ideal for UI queries and frequent polling.

Quick facts
  • No gas cost
  • No state change
  • Fast, depends on node responsiveness
send()

State change, requires gas

Broadcasts a transaction, consumes gas, and must be mined. Use for modifications and transfers.

Quick facts
  • Costs gas
  • Alters blockchain state
  • Requires confirmations to be final
Developer tip

If you expect no state change, call() is safer and cheaper. Validate the Solidity function signature before deciding.

Common mistake

Using send() on a view function will attempt a transaction and likely revert; it also wastes gas. Always use call() for read-only interactions.

screens.title: Typical call() usage pattern
screens.subtitle: How to compose contract.methods.myFunction().call() with async/await and try/catch

narration.text: The usual pattern for calling a read-only function in Web3. js uses the methods object, then call() and async/await for clean error handling. Start by creating a web3 instance and a Contract object with the ABI and deployed address. Then access the method through contract. methods. methodName(... args). call(). Because call() returns a Promise, wrap it in try/catch and await the result. This avoids returning a Promise object to the rest of your code and makes debugging clearer. For example, when you await contract. methods. retrieve(). call(), you can log the result and then convert numeric strings with parseInt or a BigNumber library. A common trap is forgetting await or failing to handle RPC errors: a node might be slow or throw an RPC error, so your UI should provide a fallback message and possibly a retry. Another small detail: call() may accept call-specific options like {from: address} in some cases, which instructs the node which account context to simulate the call under. Practice using try/catch in your frontends and include user-friendly status updates when RPC responses are delayed. Typical call() usage pattern means create contract, call method with await inside try/catch, then convert/consume the returned value safely.. In practical terms, how to compose contract.methods.myfunction().call() with async/await and try/catch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Create Contract, call method with await inside try/catch, then convert/consume the returned value safely.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Typical call() pattern
Code Walkthrough

Awaiting a call with try/catch

async function readValue(contract) {
  try {
    const raw = await contract.methods.retrieve().call();
    console.log('raw:', raw);
    const value = parseInt(raw);
    return value;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('call failed:', err.message);
    return null;
  }
}
Note: parseInt is safe only when the number is within JavaScript's safe integer range. Otherwise use a BigNumber library.
Options

You can pass an optional call context like .call({ from: someAddress }) to simulate the call using that account's context on the node.

Example
const result = await contract.methods.getCount().call({ from: accounts[0] });
Pro tip

Always handle unexpected RPC errors and display a loading state while awaiting call() to avoid confusing the user.

screens.title: Handling BigNumber and numeric returns
screens.subtitle: Why Web3.js returns strings for large integers and how to handle them safely

narration.text: When a Solidity function returns an unsigned integer like uint256, Web3. js often represents that value as a string. This is deliberate: JavaScript's Number type cannot safely represent the full 256-bit range and would lose precision. Treat those returned strings as either string-based integers or convert them using a BigNumber library when you will do arithmetic or comparisons beyond JavaScript safe limits. A practical approach: if the expected value is small (for example a counter you control and know will stay below Number. MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), you can use parseInt to convert to a Number for simple tasks. But for token balances, or any value that could exceed safe bounds, use BN. js or ethers. js BigNumber to add, subtract, and compare safely. Another misconception is assuming that converting the string with parseFloat or Number is always safe; it is not. Also remember to handle decimals carefully: Ethereum token balances are integers in Wei, so format and scale when presenting Ether or token decimals. Closing question: when you display a token balance, do you need raw arithmetic on the chain value, or will a formatting conversion to human units suffice?

keyIdea.title: Numeric safety
keyIdea.text: Returned uints are often strings; use parseInt only when safe, otherwise use BN or ethers BigNumber for math.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Handling BigNumber

Why strings for integers?

JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floating point and risk precision loss for very large integers like uint256. Web3.js returns large integers as strings to avoid silent errors.

Safe conversions
  • Use parseInt when you control or expect small values.
  • Use BN.js or ethers BigNumber for token balances and large math.
  • Always format Wei to Ether for display using web3.utils.fromWei.
Code examples
// parse small uint
const raw = await contract.methods.getCount().call();
const count = parseInt(raw); // safe if small

// use BN for large values
const balanceRaw = await token.methods.balanceOf(addr).call();
// new BN(balanceRaw) ... do arithmetic
Misconception

Do not rely on parseInt for high-value balances. Precision loss silently creates bugs in financial calculations.

screens.title: Common read-only queries in dApps
screens.subtitle: Token balances, NFT ownership, votes, and price feeds — when call() is essential

narration.text: Read-only calls power many parts of decentralized applications. Common scenarios include querying ERC-20 token balances with balanceOf(address), checking NFT ownership using ownerOf(tokenId), verifying whether a user has voted on a proposal with hasVoted(address), or reading price data from on-chain oracles via latestRoundData or similar view functions. In each case you only need the current state, not a state change, so call() is the right choice. These calls are often frequent and should be implemented with caching and sensible polling intervals to avoid overwhelming your node. Another important point is formatting: token balances are typically stored in the smallest unit (Wei or token decimals), so convert to human-friendly units before displaying. A mistake developers make is calling a read-only function on every render without debouncing; prefer a lifecycle or subscription approach that updates only when necessary. Consider whether you need the freshest value every second or whether a short cache will provide a better UX and lower node load. How might you balance freshness with performance in your own dApp? Common read-only queries in dApps means use call() for any read-only state the ui depends on; format units and cache or poll sensibly to balance freshness and load.. In practical terms, token balances, nft ownership, votes, and price feeds — when call() is essential. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Practical checks to keep your read-only calls robust

narration.text: Several mistakes recur when developers first use call(). The first is using send() by accident for a view function; that creates a transaction, consumes gas, and often reverts. The second is forgetting to await the Promise returned by call(), which leads your code to work with a Promise object rather than the expected value. Third, treating returned numeric strings as native numbers without checking safe ranges leads to silent arithmetic errors. Fourth, ignoring node latency: call() is fast, but still depends on the RPC node. Always include try/catch and present a user-facing error or retry logic. Avoid calling state-reading functions every render; use appropriate lifecycle hooks, caching, or polling strategies. For any financial values, prefer BigNumber arithmetic and format units explicitly for the user. Finally, test on different nodes: local Ganache is fast and predictable, but public nodes may have rate limits or slower responses. Add exponential backoff if you need automatic retries. These checks make your dApp resilient and predictable. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means avoid send on view functions, always await promises, handle bignumber properly, and implement robust rpc error handling.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing reads and handling RPC errors
screens.subtitle: What to assert and how to surface issues during development

narration.text: When testing read-only interactions, assert both correctness of return values and robustness to node failures. Unit tests for contract reads can run against a local test node like Ganache: assert that contract. methods. getCount(). call() returns the expected initial value and updates after a send transaction in integration tests. For frontend tests, mock the contract methods to simulate both normal responses and RPC errors. For runtime resilience, design graceful fallbacks: a loading indicator when awaiting the call and an informative error message with a retry option if the node times out. Implement exponential backoff for automated retries to avoid hammering a slow node. When debugging RPC errors, inspect error. message for JSON-RPC error codes and log the networkId and provider URL you used so problems can be reproduced. Finally, tests should include BigNumber conversion checks to ensure no precision loss. These practices help you catch subtle bugs early and present a reliable interface to your users. Testing reads and handling RPC errors means assert expected read values, mock failure cases, and add retries and clear ui feedback for rpc errors.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Second, view functions read state while pure functions do not read or write state — both are suitable for call(). Third, Web3. js often returns uint256 values as strings to avoid precision loss; use parseInt only when values are small enough, otherwise use a BigNumber library. These three ideas form the practical core: choose call() for reads, inspect function mutability in Solidity, and handle returned numbers safely. Keep these points in mind when designing frontends that query on-chain data frequently. They will keep your app fast, accurate, and cost-efficient.
